idiom_name: @Inject constructor injection resolved by a Guice injector (GuiceApplicationLoader)
implementation_notes: On the JVM, Scala uses the same JSR-330 stack as Java: constructors marked @Inject are resolved from a Guice injector that Play bootstraps through GuiceApplicationLoader and binding modules, with @Named qualifiers for competing implementations and scopes for lifetimes. What replaces the injector is this container plus its modules, and the consumer stays a plain class with trait-typed constructor parameters. Scala adds two compile-time alternatives - the Cake pattern and MacWire - that keep the same consumer side.
pitfalls: Guice builds the graph at run time: a missing binding fails on first resolution unless the injector is asserted at start-up.
Guice singletons are lazy by default; use .asEagerSingleton() for fail-fast but watch start-up order.
Circular constructor dependencies need Provider injection or restructuring - Guice cannot break a constructor cycle.

variants.name: The Cake pattern (self-typed component traits)
variants.idiom_name: self-typed component traits composed by a registry object
variants.implementation_notes: The Cake pattern composes the graph out of traits: a component trait declares the abstract val for its service and its dependencies as self-types (this: RepoComponent =>), and a final registry object mixes the components and instantiates the vals once. Resolution happens in the compiler - no reflection, no library, no runtime container - which is why it is called the idiomatic Scala DI. Choose it for small, stable graphs; it scales poorly to deep ones because every composition is written by hand and rebinding means a new mixin.
pitfalls: Every new dependency changes a trait signature and ripples through the mixins; name collisions between components are silent.
Self-type composition has initialization-order hazards for vals referencing each other - prefer lazy val or def.

variants.name: MacWire compile-time macro wiring
variants.implementation_notes: MacWire generates the new-instance wiring at compile time: wire[OrderService] expands to new OrderService(wire[OrderRepository], wire[Clock]), looking dependencies up in the enclosing trait/class/object, so the graph is type-checked with no runtime overhead and missing dependencies are compile errors. Modules are ordinary Scala traits or objects combined by inheritance or composition, and instances are lazy vals or defs whose scope the application decides. It sits between the Cake pattern and Guice in ceremony and is the common compile-time DI choice for Scala services.
pitfalls: wire looks values up by type in scope - two values of the same type need tags (scala-common @@) or explicit ascription.
Macros only see the enclosing scope; wiring inside deeply nested traits and classes is not supported.
